notes.meaning: Jesus knew that the appointed time for His death had arrived, and He viewed dying as returning home to His Father. Even as the cross drew near, His attention remained entirely on His disciples. He loved them fully and completely, and He would continue to love them to the very end of His earthly life.

While the evening meal was taking place, the devil had already suggested the wicked plan of betrayal into the heart of Judas. The text shows the terrible nature of Judas's sin, which was sparked by his own greed and driven by Satan. Jesus chose to carry out His final acts of love even while knowing that a traitor sat at the table.

Jesus was completely aware of His supreme dignity and divine power, knowing that the Father had placed all authority into His hands. He also knew that He came directly from God and was about to return to God. It was not in ignorance of His greatness, but in full consciousness of it, that He stooped down to serve.

Jesus stood up from the meal, took off His outer robe, and tied a linen towel around His waist like a common slave. He then poured water into a basin and began washing the dirty feet of His disciples, drying them with the towel. In Bible times, washing the dusty feet of guests was the work of the lowest servant, making this a stunning display of humble love.

When Jesus approached Simon Peter, Peter was shocked that his Lord would do such a menial chore. Peter's question put the spotlight on the sharp contrast between who Jesus is—the Lord and Master—and who Peter is—a lowly and sinful follower. Out of a sense of awe, Peter shrank back from letting Jesus serve him in this way.

Jesus told Peter that he could not understand the true meaning of this action right now, but he would understand it later. The foot-washing was a visual lesson that pointed forward to the cross and to spiritual cleansing, which the disciples would grasp after Jesus was raised. Believers are called to trust and obey God's actions even when they cannot see His full purpose at the time.

Peter bluntly refused to let Jesus wash his feet, showing a stubborn will disguised as modesty. Jesus answered that without this washing, Peter could have no share or fellowship with Him. Jesus was speaking of spiritual cleansing; no one can belong to Christ unless they allow Him to wash away their sins.

Fearing that he might be cut off from his Lord, Peter swung to the opposite extreme and asked Jesus to wash his hands and head as well. Peter's quick change of heart showed his deep love for Jesus, even though he still misunderstood the point of the action. A true follower of Christ desires to be made completely pure in every part of life.

Jesus explained that a person who has already bathed all over is fundamentally clean and only needs their dusty feet rinsed after walking. In the spiritual life, this means that a believer is fully justified—declared right with God and forgiven once for all—yet still needs daily confession to wash away the defilement of daily sins. Jesus added that they were clean, but not all of them, because He already knew that Judas was going to betray Him.

After putting His robe back on and returning to the table, Jesus asked if they understood what He had done. He confirmed that He truly is their Teacher and Lord, but pointed out that their Master had just performed the lowest task for them. Therefore, they were obligated to follow His pattern and serve one another with that same lowly, self-giving love.

differ.view: Certain groups, such as the Church of the Brethren and some Baptists, view foot-washing as a third church ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord's Supper, to be practiced literally.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Foot-washing is retained as a liturgical rite on Holy Thursday to express Christ's humility, but is not counted as a sacrament.

notes.meaning: Jesus reminded His followers that a servant is never greater than his master, nor is an ambassador greater than the one who sent him. If the Lord of heaven was willing to stoop to the ground to serve, His followers should never think any act of loving kindness is beneath them. Real joy and divine blessing do not come simply from knowing the truth, but from putting it into daily practice.

Jesus made clear that His promise of blessing did not apply to all twelve men, because He knew those He had chosen for salvation. The treachery of Judas was no surprise or failure of Jesus' plan, but happened to fulfill the ancient prophecy in Psalm 41:9. In ancient culture, sharing bread was a pledge of close friendship, making Judas's sudden turn against Jesus especially cruel and hateful.

Jesus foretold this betrayal before it actually happened so that the disciples would not lose their faith when the arrest took place. When they saw everything unfold exactly as He had warned, their trust in Him would be strengthened. They would know with certainty that He is the true Messiah who sees all things ahead of time.

Jesus encouraged the faithful apostles by reassuring them of the dignity of their holy mission. Anyone who welcomes the messenger Christ sends is actually welcoming Christ Himself, and welcoming Christ is welcoming the Father who sent Him. Even though one apostle was a traitor, the true calling of the others remained sacred and backed by God's own authority.

After giving these warnings, Jesus experienced deep anguish and sorrow in His inner spirit. He spoke with solemn certainty, openly declaring that one of His own close companions at the table was going to hand Him over to His enemies. Christ felt genuine human grief over the cold-hearted betrayal of a friend.

The disciples looked around at one another in utter confusion and distress, completely at a loss as to who could do such a thing. Because they trusted their Master completely, they knew the warning was true, but they could not spot the traitor among them. Judas had hidden his evil plans so well under a show of religion that none of his fellow apostles suspected him.

John, who modestly referred to himself as the disciple Jesus loved, was reclining right next to Jesus on the dining couch. Simon Peter made a discreet signal to John, urging him to ask the Lord who the traitor was. Leaning his head back close to Jesus' chest, John whispered the private question, asking Him to name the person.

Jesus answered John quietly by giving a specific sign: the betrayer would be the one to whom He handed a dipped piece of bread. He then dipped the morsel into the dish and handed it directly to Judas. Offering a piece of food was an ordinary gesture of honor and hospitality at a meal, giving Judas one final, tender appeal to turn from his wickedness.

As soon as Judas took the morsel without repenting, Satan took complete control of his heart and hardened his wicked resolve. Jesus then looked at Judas and told him to go do what he was about to do without delay. Jesus was not commanding the sin itself, but was dismissing the unrepentant traitor and showing that He was willingly offering Himself up to die.

No one else at the table understood what Jesus meant by those words, because they had not heard His private exchange with John. Since Judas carried the common money purse for the group, some disciples assumed Jesus was sending him to buy food for the feast or to give money to the poor. Even in His own poverty, Jesus routinely set aside money to care for those in need.

Judas ate the piece of bread and hurried straight out of the room to carry out his dark plot with the chief priests. John notes that it was night, which pointed to the actual darkness of the evening as well as the deep spiritual darkness that now ruled Judas's soul. When a person turns away from Christ, they step out into total spiritual blindness.

Once the traitor had left the room, Jesus proclaimed that the Son of Man was now glorified, and God was glorified in Him. Although the cross seemed like a place of terrible shame, Jesus saw it as His greatest victory, where God's holy justice and infinite mercy would be displayed to all creation. Because the Son honored the Father by obeying unto death, the Father would immediately honor and exalt the Son in His resurrection.

Using the tender title of 'little children,' Jesus spoke with the warmth and care of a father who is about to leave his family. He told them that He would be with them only a very short time, and that they could not come where He was going. While unbelievers were shut out forever because of their sins, these disciples were only separated from Him for a little while until their work on earth was finished.

Jesus gave His disciples a new commandment: they must love one another just as He had loved them. Loving one's neighbor was an old law in the Old Testament, but it was now new in its standard and pattern, which was Christ's own self-sacrificing love on the cross. Believers are called to pour out their lives for one another with that same patient, costly devotion.

Jesus declared that mutual love would be the distinct uniform and badge by which the entire world would recognize His followers. Other religious groups were known by special robes, diets, or outward rituals, but Christians were to be set apart by their genuine love for each other. When Christians fail to show love, they hurt the witness of the gospel and give people reason to doubt their faith.

Peter skipped over the command about love and asked where Jesus was going, still troubled by the thought of being left behind. Jesus answered that Peter could not follow Him right now, but would follow Him later on. Peter was not yet ready for the hardship of the cross, but years later he would indeed follow Jesus into martyrdom and heavenly glory.

Peter pressed his question further, wondering why he was considered unfit to follow his Master immediately. In a burst of sincere but reckless confidence, he claimed that he was ready to die and lay down his life for Jesus. Peter truly loved the Lord, but he relied on his own human courage instead of depending on God's strength.

Jesus gently challenged Peter's proud boast and revealed how frail his human strength really was. He solemnly warned him that before the rooster finished crowing that very night, Peter would deny knowing Him three separate times. Christ knows the weakness of His saints far better than they know themselves, reminding believers to walk humbly and rely completely on His grace.
